name: Colloidal silver
lead: Colloidal silver is a suspension of tiny silver particles in a liquid, often described as nanosilver when particles are below 100 nanometres. It is promoted in some alternative-health circles as an ingestible or topical health and immune aid, and it is marketed online as a dietary supplement.[1][2][13]

Its connection to appearance runs in one direction: argyria, a blue-grey discolouration of skin, nails, gums and other tissues that can follow chronic ingestion, inhalation or topical use of silver, including colloidal silver. Wikipedia and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health describe it as usually permanent, and it is the best-documented visible effect of the product.[4][13] Cases that reach the media are usually accounts of argyria, such as that of Paul Karason.[4][14]

Wikipedia says colloidal silver has been marketed for cancer, diabetes, arthritis, HIV/AIDS, herpes and tuberculosis, and that no medical evidence supports these claims.[1] NCCIH states the FDA has said colloidal silver is not safe or effective for treating any disease, and that the FDA and FTC have acted against companies making misleading claims.[13] Silver in dressings and sinus irrigations has been investigated separately, and reviews state nanosilver is not inert in the body.[2][5][6]

FDA says not safe or effective for any disease; EPA classes antimicrobial silver nanoparticles as pesticides [1][13]

paras: Wikipedia describes silver nanoparticles as particles between 1 and 100 nm, many of which are used as a colloid, and says that M. C. Lea made a citrate-stabilised silver colloid in 1889. Promotion of colloidal silver as a dietary supplement resumed around 1990 [1]. A 2011 analysis found that colloidal silver had been used for more than 100 years and registered as a biocidal material in the United States since 1954 [7].

Silver compounds were used for infections and wounds before antibiotics. Wikipedia says doctors recorded grey discolouration from silver from the mid-1800s, and that colloidal silver fell from use as an internal medicine in the 1940s once penicillin and other antibiotics arrived.[4] The NCCIH notes some colloidal silver products are sold as homeopathic remedies.[13]

Wikipedia reports claims that colloidal silver can prevent or treat conditions including cancer, diabetes, arthritis, HIV/AIDS, herpes and tuberculosis, and states that silver is not an essential mineral for humans [1]. A 2015 review notes that colloidal silver is considered by many to be an ideal agent against pathogens without the side effects of antibiotics, but that toxicological research indicates nanosilver is not inert in the body [2].

Argyria happens when light decomposes pale silver compounds into silver metal or silver sulfides that deposit as microscopic particles in the skin and act like a dark pigment, most visibly on sun-exposed areas. It can be generalised or local to patches, mucous membranes or the conjunctiva.[4] Wikipedia describes it as cosmetically undesirable and not life-threatening, with research on possible kidney and night-vision effects not definitive, and says it worsens with continued exposure and persists after exposure ends because silver cannot be removed from tissue.[4]

NCCIH adds that colloidal silver can interfere with absorption of some drugs such as certain antibiotics and thyroxine, and that there is some evidence of kidney, liver or nervous-system problems.[13]

Wikipedia and NCCIH describe publicised cases. Stan Jones, a Libertarian US Senate candidate in 2002 and 2006, said he took colloidal silver out of Y2K worries about antibiotic supply.[4] Paul Karason (1950 to 2013), a Bellingham, Washington man, began in the early 1990s taking a homemade colloidal silver and rubbing a silver preparation on his skin for sinus problems, dermatitis and acid reflux, and his skin turned blue. He appeared on NBC's Today in 2008, said silver relieved his conditions while acknowledging it caused his argyria, and kept using it until his death in 2013 after a heart attack, pneumonia and a stroke; coverage cited by Wikipedia questioned whether the discolouration contributed to his death.[14][4] Rosemary Jacobs developed argyria from childhood nose drops containing colloidal silver and later became a prominent critic of alternative medicine.[4]
Earlier descriptions of grey or blue-grey skin from silver appear in medical publications from 1843 and 1859.[4]

A 2015 occupational review reported that inhaled silver nanoparticles had adverse effects mainly on the liver and lungs of rats, via oxidative stress [2], and a 2014 review examined oral toxicity of silver ions, nanoparticles and colloidal silver [8]. The US EPA classifies silver nanoparticles used for antimicrobial purposes as pesticides [1].

The NCCIH reports that the FDA has warned colloidal silver is not safe or effective for treating any disease or condition, and that the FDA and FTC have taken action against companies making misleading claims.[13] The US EPA classifies silver nanoparticles used for antimicrobial purposes as pesticides, and the substance has been registered as a biocide in the US since 1954.[1][7] Wikipedia lists silver as not an essential mineral for humans.[1]

No studies found on ingesting colloidal silver for appearance. Human studies of silver products for other purposes include a controlled study in which an orally taken commercial colloidal silver product produced detectable serum silver after 14 days but no clinically significant changes in metabolic, blood, urinary or physical findings or in cytochrome P450 enzyme activity [6]. A placebo-controlled study examined commercial silver nanoparticles and ex vivo platelet aggregation [9]. Randomised trials have examined topical colloidal silver in recalcitrant chronic rhinosinusitis and a colloidal silver device for upper airway disease in children [10][11], and reviews describe colloidal silver irrigation as a novel treatment under investigation for sinus infection whose evidence base is limited [5][12].

Colloidal silver is a minor topic in appearance communities compared with other wellness practices. It appears mostly as a cautionary example, because argyria is visible and does not fade, and as an ingredient in alternative skin and sinus remedies. Wikipedia reports that local argyria often follows topical use, such as certain eye drops, and that reviews describe silver dressings and sinus irrigations as investigated medical uses.[4][5][12]

lore.intro: Claims about colloidal silver circulate in alternative-health communities and are reported on Wikipedia and by NCCIH; the appearance conversation centres on argyria.[1][13]

claims.claim: Ingesting colloidal silver treats or prevents illness
claims.believers: Promoters market it as an immune or antimicrobial supplement for conditions ranging from infections to cancer [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports colloidal silver for any claimed use and that silver is not an essential mineral [1]. NCCIH reports FDA statements that colloidal silver is not safe or effective for treating any disease.[13]

claims.claim: Colloidal silver has no side effects
claims.believers: Some advocates consider it an ideal antimicrobial agent without the side effects of antibiotics [2].
claims.experts: A review says nanosilver is not inert in the body, and Wikipedia reports that chronic ingestion can cause permanent argyria [2][4].

claims.claim: Silver can be taken safely in small amounts for skin or sinus health
claims.believers: Users of homemade or commercial silver describe benefits for sinus problems, dermatitis and reflux; Paul Karason said silver helped his conditions.[14]
claims.experts: NCCIH states silver has no known benefit when taken by mouth and that a few nasal-spray studies showed no meaningful improvement in chronic sinus infections.[13]

claims.believers: Some users regard a bluish tint as cosmetic only.[14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and NCCIH describe argyria as usually permanent and not reversing after exposure stops.[4][13]

claims.believers: Marketing has presented it as one.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and NCCIH say silver is not essential for humans.[1][13]

card.summary: Ingested silver suspension sold as a health supplement; claims are unsupported per Wikipedia and chronic use can cause permanent blue-grey skin (argyria).
card.note: Argyria is described as permanent once it develops.

quick.overview:
Colloidal silver is a suspension of very small silver particles that some alternative-health sources promote as a supplement to ingest for immunity and illness. It has a long history as an antimicrobial and was registered as a biocide in the US in 1954.

Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports it for the claimed uses, and silver is not an essential mineral. Its most visible documented effect on appearance is argyria, a lasting blue-grey skin colour.
quick.mechanism: Silver particles have antimicrobial properties in laboratory and wound-dressing contexts, and are used in medical devices and textiles. Reviews say ingested nanosilver is not inert and distributes to tissues such as the liver.
quick.risks: Chronic ingestion or inhalation of silver can cause argyria, which Wikipedia says does not resolve after exposure stops. Reviews report liver and lung effects of inhaled nanosilver in rats, and the US EPA classifies antimicrobial silver nanoparticles as pesticides.
